mainTopic: בישולי גוים: its rabbinic source, which foods it covers, and when a non-Jew's involvement in cooking makes food forbidden.
overview: The גמרא first concludes that the ban on בישולי גוים is only מדרבנן, and that the פסוק is just an אסמכתא. רב's rule on which foods are covered was taught two ways. סורא taught that food eaten raw is not included. פומבדיתא taught that food not served at a king's table is not included. Small fish, mushrooms and porridge show the difference between them. רב יוסף adds that salted fish roasted by a non-Jew are permitted, but fish fried with flour (כסא דהרסנא) is forbidden, because the flour is the main ingredient. The גמרא then explains that locusts burned when a גוי set fire to a meadow are forbidden only because kosher and non-kosher kinds get mixed up. They are not בישולי גוים, since a גוי who is not trying to cook does not make food forbidden, as with the singed head and רבינא's peg in the oven. Finally, שמואל rules that meat a ישראל put on coals stays permitted even if a גוי turned it over and made it cook faster. A ברייתא supports this ruling and continues on the next amud.

steps.title: The ban on non-Jewish cooking is rabbinic
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא concludes that בישולי גוים is forbidden only מדרבנן, and the פסוק is just a supporting hint.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, it is forbidden by rabbinic law, and the verse is only a supporting hint.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא is closing the earlier discussion. It decides that the ban on בישולי גוים comes from the חכמים, not from the תורה.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Earlier, the גמרא had looked at a פסוק as if it might be a תורה source for this ban. Now it says the ban is really מדרבנן. The פסוק is only an אסמכתא, a hint the חכמים 'leaned on.' Because the ban is rabbinic, the חכמים can decide exactly which foods it covers, and the rest of this section does just that.

keyTerms.meaning: By rabbinic law (not from the תורה itself)
A verse used only as a hint or support, not as the real source

steps.whatToRemember: בישולי גוים is a rabbinic ban. The פסוק is only an אסמכתא.
steps.confusionAlert: When the גמרא quotes a פסוק next to a law, it does not always mean the law comes from the תורה. Here the גמרא says outright that the פסוק is only a hint.

phrases.english: Rather, it is by rabbinic law,
and the verse is merely a support.
phrases.notes: The פסוק from just before (דברים 2:28) is only being used as a hint.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Closes the discussion from the previous daf about whether the ban comes from the תורה.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: בישולי גוים is מדרבנן, and the פסוק is only an אסמכתא.

steps.title: סורא version: food eaten raw is not included
steps.stepSummary: רב שמואל בר רב יצחק quotes רב: any food that can be eaten raw is not covered by בישולי גוים.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב שמואל בר רב יצחק said in the name of רב: Anything that is eaten as it is, raw, is not included in the ban on food cooked by non-Jews.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא now starts defining which foods the ban covers. This first version says that if a food can be eaten raw, cooking it does not make it forbidden.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The idea is simple. If people already eat this food raw, the non-Jew's cooking did not really 'make' it into food, so the חכמים did not forbid it. The test here is the food itself: can it be eaten without cooking?

keyTerms.meaning: Food cooked by a non-Jew, which the חכמים forbade
As it is, in its present state
It is not included in (a certain ban)

phrases.aramaic: אָמַר רַב שְׁמוּאֵל בַּר רַב יִצְחָק אָמַר רַב:
phrases.english: Rav Shmuel bar Rav Yitzchak said that Rav said:
Anything that is eaten as it is, raw —
is not subject to the ban on food cooked by non-Jews.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַב שְׁמוּאֵל בַּר רַב יִצְחָק אָמַר רַב: כָּל הַנֶּאֱכָל כְּמוֹת שֶׁהוּא חַי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Now that the ban is known to be rabbinic, the גמרא begins defining its limits.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Food that is edible raw is not covered by בישולי גוים.

steps.title: פומבדיתא version: food not fit for a king's table is not included
steps.stepSummary: In סורא, רב's rule was taught as in step 2. In פומבדיתא it was taught differently: any food not served with bread at a king's table is not covered.
steps.simpleTranslation: In סורא they taught it this way. In פומבדיתא they taught it this way: רב שמואל בר רב יצחק said in the name of רב: Anything that is not eaten on the table of kings together with bread is not included in the ban on food cooked by non-Jews.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא reports that the two big yeshivos remembered רב's rule differently. פומבדיתא's version gives a different test: is this an important food that would be served to a king?
steps.deeperAnalysis: The ban was made to keep Jews from becoming close to non-Jews over meals. So פומבדיתא's version looks at how important the food is. A simple food would never be served at a fancy meal, so it is not included. This is a different test from סורא's 'can it be eaten raw?' test.

keyTerms.meaning: The table of kings, meaning an important, fancy meal
To eat it together with bread, as a side dish

steps.confusionAlert: This is not a disagreement between two אמוראים. It is the same rule, quoted by the same person in the name of רב, but remembered in two different ways by two ישיבות.

phrases.english: In Sura they taught it this way;
in Pumbedita they taught it this way:

phrases.aramaic: אָמַר רַב שְׁמוּאֵל בַּר רַב יִצְחָק אָמַר רַב:
phrases.english: Rav Shmuel bar Rav Yitzchak said that Rav said:

phrases.aramaic: כׇּל שֶׁאֵינוֹ נֶאֱכָל עַל שׁוּלְחַן מְלָכִים
phrases.english: Anything that is not eaten on the table of kings
together with bread —
is not subject to the ban on food cooked by non-Jews.

steps.triggerLanguage: בְּסוּרָא מַתְנוּ הָכִי, בְּפוּמְבְּדִיתָא מַתְנוּ הָכִי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives a second version of the same statement from step 2, with a different test.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Food not important enough for a king's table is not covered by בישולי גוים.

steps.title: What is the difference between the two versions?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks what practical difference there is between the סורא and פומבדיתא versions.
steps.simpleTranslation: What is the difference between them?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks a clarifying question. It is setting up the next step, which will name foods where the two versions give different answers.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Most foods come out the same way under both tests. The גמרא wants a case where one test forbids the food and the other permits it.

keyTerms.meaning: What is the difference between them?

phrases.english: What is the difference between them?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Compares the two versions just given.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: A practical case where the סורא and פומבדיתא versions lead to different rulings.

steps.title: Small fish, mushrooms, and porridge
steps.stepSummary: The difference shows up with small fish, mushrooms, and porridge. These foods are not eaten raw, but they are also not fit for a king's table.
steps.simpleTranslation: There is a difference between them regarding small fish, mushrooms, and porridge.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers its question. It names three foods that come out differently under the two versions.
steps.deeperAnalysis: These foods are not eaten raw, so under סורא's test they are forbidden when a non-Jew cooks them. But they are simple foods that a king would not serve, so under פומבדיתא's test they are permitted.

keyTerms.meaning: There is a difference between them

steps.whatToRemember: סורא: food eaten raw is not covered. פומבדיתא: food not fit for a king's table is not covered. Small fish, mushrooms, and porridge are forbidden according to סורא and permitted according to פומבדיתא.

phrases.english: There is a difference between them:
small fish, mushrooms, and porridge.

steps.triggerLanguage: אִיכָּא בֵּינַיְיהוּ: דָּגִים קְטַנִּים, וְאַרְדֵי, וְדַיְיסָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question from step 4.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: Small fish, mushrooms, and porridge are not eaten raw but are not fit for kings, so the two versions disagree about them.

steps.title: Small salted fish are not included
steps.stepSummary: רב אסי quotes רב: small fish that have been salted are not covered by בישולי גוים.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב אסי said in the name of רב: Small salted fish are not included in the ban on food cooked by non-Jews.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a new statement about one specific food: small fish that were salted.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Plain small fish were just listed as forbidden according to סורא, because they are not eaten raw. Once they are salted, though, they are already edible without cooking. So cooking them does not count as בישולי גוים.

phrases.english: Rav Asi said that Rav said:
Small salted fish
are not subject to the ban on food cooked by non-Jews.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַב אַסִּי אָמַר רַב: דָּגִים קְטַנִּים מְלוּחִים
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Picks up 'small fish' from step 5 and gives the rule for salted ones.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Small salted fish are not covered by בישולי גוים.

steps.title: Roasted salted fish and fish fried in batter
steps.stepSummary: רב יוסף: if a non-Jew roasted small salted fish, a Jew may use them for ערובי תבשילין. If the non-Jew made them into כסא דהרסנא, they are forbidden.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב יוסף said: If a non-Jew roasted them, a Jew may rely on them for ערובי תבשילין. But if a non-Jew made them into כסא דהרסנא, it is forbidden.
steps.whatsHappening: רב יוסף adds two practical rules about these salted fish. Roasted ones are permitted and even count as a cooked food. Ones made into a fried dish with flour are forbidden.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Roasting does not make the fish forbidden, because salted fish are already edible. Yet roasting still makes them a 'cooked food,' so they can serve as the cooked dish for ערובי תבשילין. כסא דהרסנא, fish fried in oil with flour, is different. The flour was not edible before cooking, so the dish counts as בישולי גוים and is forbidden.

keyTerms.meaning: A cooked dish set aside before יום טוב so one may cook on יום טוב for שבת
A dish of small fish fried in oil with flour

steps.whatToRemember: Salted small fish are not covered by בישולי גוים. Once roasted, they even count as cooked food for ערובי תבשילין. But when fried with flour as כסא דהרסנא, they are forbidden.
steps.whyThisMatters: This shows that whether a food is forbidden as בישולי גוים depends on what the cooking actually did to the food. That includes added ingredients like flour, which were not edible before cooking.

phrases.english: Rav Yosef said:
If a non-Jew roasted them,
phrases.notes: 'Them' means the small salted fish from the step before.

phrases.english: a Jew may rely on them
for the eruv tavshilin;
but if a non-Jew made them into kasa deharsena —
it is forbidden.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַב יוֹסֵף: אִם צְלָאָן גּוֹי סוֹמֵךְ יִשְׂרָאֵל עֲלֵיהֶם מִשּׁוּם עֵירוּבֵי תַבְשִׁילִין
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Builds on רב's rule about small salted fish and applies it to two ways of cooking them.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Roasted salted fish made by a non-Jew are permitted and count as cooked food for ערובי תבשילין. When fried with flour as כסא דהרסנא, they are forbidden.

steps.title: Isn't that obvious?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks why רב יוסף needed to say that כסא דהרסנא made by a גוי is forbidden. That seems obvious.
steps.simpleTranslation: Isn't that obvious?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא questions the second half of רב יוסף's ruling from step 7. Why would anyone think a cooked flour-and-fish dish made by a גוי is allowed?
steps.deeperAnalysis: כסא דהרסנא is a cooked dish, so of course it falls under בישולי גוים. The גמרא wants to know what new point רב יוסף was teaching.

keyTerms.meaning: It is obvious, so why say it?

phrases.english: It is obvious!
phrases.notes: This points back to רב יוסף's ruling that כסא דהרסנא made by a גוי is forbidden.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the need for the second half of רב יוסף's statement.
steps.kashyaTarget: רב יוסף's ruling that כסא דהרסנא is forbidden
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: A cooked dish made by a גוי is plainly בישולי גוים, so the ruling seems to teach nothing new.

steps.title: The flour is the main ingredient, not the fish
steps.stepSummary: We might have thought the salted fish (which is allowed) is the main part of the dish. רב יוסף teaches that the flour is the main part.
steps.simpleTranslation: You might have said the salted fish is the main part. He teaches us that the flour is the main part.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the 'obvious' question. רב יוסף's ruling teaches which ingredient decides the status of the dish.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Step 6 said salted small fish are not covered by בישולי גוים. So one might think a dish built on that fish is also allowed. רב יוסף teaches that the flour decides the status, and cooked flour is covered by בישולי גוים.

keyTerms.meaning: You might have said (the mistaken first idea)
The main part, which decides the status of the whole

phrases.english: You might have said: the salted fish is the main part,
phrases.notes: Salted small fish were allowed even when a גוי cooked them (step 6). That is why someone could make this mistake.

phrases.english: so he teaches us: the flour is the main part.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the 'obvious' question from step 8.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Shows the ruling is not obvious by naming a reasonable mistaken idea
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The salted fish is the main part, so the dish would be allowed like the fish itself.
steps.terutzMaskana: The flour is the main part, so the dish is forbidden as בישולי גוים.
steps.whatToRemember: In a mixed dish, the main ingredient (עיקר) decides whether it falls under בישולי גוים. In כסא דהרסנא, that is the flour.

steps.title: A גוי set fire to a meadow: the locusts are forbidden
steps.stepSummary: רב ברונא quotes רב: if a גוי lit a fire in a meadow, all the locusts in it are forbidden.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב ברונא said in the name of רב: if a גוי set fire to a meadow, all the locusts in the meadow are forbidden.
steps.whatsHappening: A new ruling is brought about locusts that were roasted when a גוי burned a meadow. The ruling does not give its reason, and the next steps will look for one.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Some kinds of locusts are kosher, and the fire effectively roasted them. The ruling says they are all forbidden but does not say why. That gap drives the rest of the discussion.

phrases.english: Rav Beruna said that Rav said:
a gentile who lit a fire in a meadow —
all the locusts in the meadow are forbidden.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Opens a new case connected to the topic of בישולי גוים.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Locusts in a meadow burned by a גוי are all forbidden.

steps.title: Why are they forbidden? Not just because of a mix-up
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks for the case. If the reason were that we can't tell kosher from non-kosher, a Jew's fire would do the same, so why mention a גוי?
steps.simpleTranslation: What is the case? If you say it is because we don't know which are kosher and which are not, why speak of a גוי? Even a Jew would cause the same problem!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא tries to figure out the reason behind רב ברונא's ruling. It tests one possible reason and pushes it aside.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Once the locusts are burnt, maybe no one can tell the kosher kinds from the non-kosher ones. But that problem has nothing to do with who lit the fire. So the word 'גוי' in the ruling would be pointless.

keyTerms.meaning: What is the case? What exactly is going on?

phrases.english: What is the case?

phrases.aramaic: אִילֵּימָא דְּלָא יָדַע הֵי טָהוֹר וְהֵי טָמֵא,
phrases.english: If you say it is because one does not know which are kosher and which are not,
why specifically a gentile?
Even a Jew as well!
phrases.notes: He means: if a Jew lit the fire, the burnt locusts would be just as mixed up.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Asks for the reason behind step 10's ruling.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: What is the reason the locusts are forbidden, and why does the ruling mention a גוי?

steps.title: The reason must be בישולי גוים
steps.stepSummary: Since a mix-up would not explain why a גוי is mentioned, the reason must be בישולי גוים.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, it is because of בישולי גוים.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא settles on a reason that fits the mention of a גוי: the locusts count as food cooked by a גוי.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Here the locusts are all kosher. They are forbidden only because a גוי's fire roasted them. This explains why the ruling says 'גוי', but the next step will challenge it.

keyTerms.meaning: Food cooked by a non-Jew, which the Rabbis forbade

phrases.english: Rather, it is because of the cooking of gentiles.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives the reason that step 11 was searching for.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The locusts are forbidden as בישולי גוים, because a גוי's fire roasted them.

steps.title: Challenge from the singed head: the גוי didn't mean to cook
steps.stepSummary: רבי יוחנן allows eating an animal head a גוי singed, even the cooked ear tip, because he only meant to remove hair. Here too, the גוי only meant to clear the meadow.
steps.simpleTranslation: Is something like this really forbidden? רב חנן בר אמי said in the name of רבי פדת in the name of רבי יוחנן: if a גוי singed an animal's head, one may eat from it, even from the tip of the ear. This shows that he only meant to remove the hair. Here too, he only meant to clear the meadow!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא attacks the בישולי גוים explanation from step 12, using a ruling of רבי יוחנן.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי יוחנן's case shows that בישולי גוים does not apply when the גוי was not trying to cook the food. Even the ear tip, which really did get cooked, is allowed. A גוי burning a meadow is trying to clear the land, not cook locusts, so they should be allowed too.
steps.confusionAlert: The ear tip really was cooked, and it is still allowed. What matters is what the גוי was trying to do, not only what happened to the food.

phrases.english: Is it forbidden in a case like this?
But didn't Rav Ḥanan bar Ami say

phrases.aramaic: אָמַר רַבִּי פְּדָת אָמַר רַבִּי יוֹחָנָן:
phrases.english: that Rabbi Pedat said that Rabbi Yoḥanan said:
this gentile who singed the head (of an animal)
it is permitted to eat from it,
even from the tip of its ear.
phrases.notes: The ear tip is thin, so the fire cooks it fully. Even so, it is allowed.

phrases.english: This shows that he intends to remove the hair,

phrases.aramaic: הָכָא נָמֵי לְגַלּוֹיֵי אַגְמָא קָא מִיכַּוֵּין!
phrases.english: here too he intends to clear the meadow!

steps.triggerLanguage: כִּי הַאי גַּוְונָא מִי אֲסִיר? וְהָאָמַר
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the בישולי גוים reason given in step 12.
steps.kashyaTarget: The explanation that the locusts are forbidden because of בישולי גוים
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: רבי יוחנן shows there is no בישולי גוים when the גוי did not mean to cook. Here the גוי only meant to clear the meadow.

steps.title: Back to the mix-up: the גוי is mentioned only because that is what happened
steps.stepSummary: The real reason is that we can't tell kosher from non-kosher locusts. A גוי is mentioned only because the actual event involved a גוי.
steps.simpleTranslation: Really, it is because one does not know which are kosher and which are not. And the reason a גוי is mentioned is that the incident that happened involved a גוי.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא goes back to the first explanation it had pushed aside. It also answers the question 'why mention a גוי?'
steps.deeperAnalysis: The בישולי גוים reason failed because the גוי did not mean to cook. So the reason is the kosher/non-kosher mix-up after all. The word 'גוי' is not part of the rule; it just describes the real incident. A Jew's fire would forbid the locusts just the same.

keyTerms.meaning: Really, in fact (going back to an earlier idea)

steps.whatToRemember: The burnt locusts are forbidden because the kosher and non-kosher ones can't be told apart, not because of בישולי גוים. A גוי who only meant to clear land is not 'cooking'.
steps.whyThisMatters: This step shows that בישולי גוים depends on the גוי meaning to cook. Food that gets cooked as a side effect of some other goal is not included.

phrases.aramaic: לְעוֹלָם, דְּלָא יָדַע הֵי טָהוֹר וְהֵי טָמֵא,
phrases.english: Actually, it is because one does not know which are kosher and which are not,
and the incident that happened, happened with a gentile.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers step 13 by dropping the בישולי גוים reason and returning to the mix-up reason from step 11.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Returns to the rejected explanation and explains away the detail that caused its rejection
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The locusts are forbidden as בישולי גוים, which is why a גוי is mentioned.
steps.terutzMaskana: They are forbidden because kosher and non-kosher kinds can't be told apart. The גוי is mentioned only because that is how the incident happened.

steps.title: Back to the statement about a singed animal head
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא returns to the statement that רבה בר בר חנה said in the name of רבי יוחנן: a head singed by a גוי may be eaten, even the cooked tip of the ear.
steps.simpleTranslation: Now the statement itself: רבה בר בר חנה said in the name of רבי יוחנן: If a גוי singed an animal's head, you may eat from it, even from the tip of the ear.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא goes back to the statement it quoted a moment ago and now looks at it on its own. This sets up רבינא's ruling that builds on it.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Earlier, in step 13, this statement was only used to push back on the idea that the locusts were forbidden as בישולי גוים. Now the גמרא studies the statement itself. The idea is that when a גוי heats food only to remove hair, the food is not counted as his cooking, even where part of it got fully cooked.

keyTerms.meaning: 'The thing itself': the גמרא goes back to discuss a statement it quoted earlier
Singed, burned off hair with fire
The tip of its ear, the part that gets fully cooked

phrases.english: The matter itself:
phrases.notes: The גמרא now goes back to the statement it quoted in step 13 so it can study it on its own.

phrases.english: Rabba bar bar Ḥana said
that Rabbi Yoḥanan said:
This gentile who singed the head of an animal,
it is permitted to eat from it,
even from the tip of its ear.

steps.triggerLanguage: גּוּפָא, אָמַר רַבָּה בַּר בַּר חָנָה אָמַר רַבִּי יוֹחָנָן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Picks up the statement used as a challenge in step 13 and makes it the new topic.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A head singed by a גוי to remove hair may be eaten, even the fully cooked ear tip, because he did not mean to cook it.

steps.title: רבינא applies the rule to a peg put into an oven
steps.stepSummary: רבינא concludes that if a גוי put a peg into an oven where a ישראל had already placed a gourd, the gourd is allowed.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבינא said: So, if a גוי threw a peg into an oven, and a ישראל had already put a gourd in there from the start, it is fine.
steps.whatsHappening: רבינא draws a practical ruling from רבי יוחנן's rule about the singed head.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The fire the גוי adds helps cook the gourd. But the גוי was only working on his peg, not cooking food. So, just like the singed head, the gourd does not become בישולי גוים.

keyTerms.meaning: It is fine, it is permitted

phrases.english: Ravina said: Therefore,
this gentile who threw a peg into the oven,
phrases.notes: He puts a wet wooden peg into the hot oven to dry it out and harden it.

phrases.english: and a Jew had placed a gourd in it from the start,
it is fine.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Applies רבי יוחנן's principle about intent to a new practical case.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A ישראל's gourd in an oven stays permitted when a גוי adds a peg to the oven only to harden it.

steps.title: Isn't that obvious?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks why רבינא needed to say this, since it seems to follow plainly from רבי יוחנן.
steps.simpleTranslation: Isn't that obvious?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges רבינא's ruling as unnecessary. This sets up the explanation of what his ruling adds.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי יוחנן already taught that when a גוי is not trying to cook food, the food is allowed. Here the גוי is not even touching the gourd, so the ruling seems to add nothing new.

keyTerms.meaning: It is obvious! Why say it at all?

phrases.english: That is obvious!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Questions whether רבינא's ruling adds anything.
steps.kashyaTarget: רבינא's ruling about the peg and the gourd
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: If a singed head is allowed, then a gourd the גוי never meant to touch is surely allowed, so the ruling seems pointless.

steps.title: The גוי means to harden the peg, not cook it
steps.stepSummary: The ruling is needed because you might think the גוי is 'cooking' his peg. רבינא teaches that he is only hardening it.
steps.simpleTranslation: You might have said he intends to cook (soften) the vessel. So רבינא teaches us that he intends to harden the vessel.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא explains what new point רבינא's ruling teaches.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Someone could think the גוי is doing a kind of cooking, softening the wet peg, so the oven counts as his cooking oven and the gourd becomes his cooking. רבינא teaches that his goal is to dry and harden the peg, which is not cooking at all.

keyTerms.meaning: You might have said, you might have thought
A vessel or object, here the peg

steps.whatToRemember: What counts is what the גוי is trying to do. If he is not trying to cook, the food heated along the way is not בישולי גוים.

phrases.english: Lest you say:
he intends to cook the vessel,
phrases.notes: 'Cooking' the peg here means softening it with heat.

phrases.english: it teaches us:
he intends to harden the vessel.

steps.triggerLanguage: מַהוּ דְּתֵימָא: לְבַשּׁוֹלֵי מָנָא קָא מִיכַּוֵּין
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the 'obvious' challenge by showing a possible mistake the ruling prevents.
steps.terutzResolutionType: מהו דתימא: shows the ruling blocks a reasonable wrong assumption
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The גוי is softening ('cooking') the peg, so his heating counts as cooking.
steps.terutzMaskana: He is only hardening the peg, so nothing he does counts as cooking.

steps.title: A גוי turns over meat a ישראל put on coals
steps.stepSummary: רב יהודה says in the name of שמואל: if a ישראל put meat on coals and a גוי turned it over, the meat is permitted.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב יהודה said in the name of שמואל: If a ישראל placed meat on coals, and a גוי came and turned it over, it is permitted.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a new ruling about meat cooked partly by a ישראל and partly by a גוי.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Here the גוי does touch the food and helps it cook, unlike the peg case. Still, שמואל says the meat stays permitted because the ישראל started the cooking.

phrases.english: Rav Yehuda said that Shmuel said:

phrases.aramaic: הִנִּיחַ יִשְׂרָאֵל בָּשָׂר עַל גַּבֵּי גֶּחָלִים,
phrases.english: If a Jew placed meat on top of coals,
and a gentile came and turned it over,
it is permitted.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Opens a new case on בישולי גוים: food cooked jointly by a ישראל and a גוי.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Meat a ישראל put on coals stays permitted even if a גוי turned it over.

steps.title: What is the case? If it would have cooked anyway, it's obvious
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks for the exact case. If the meat would have cooked even without the turning, the ruling is obvious.
steps.simpleTranslation: What is the case? If you say that even if he hadn't turned it, it would have cooked, then it's obvious!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא starts working out exactly which case שמואל meant. It tries a first option and rejects it as too obvious.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If the meat would have cooked fully without the גוי, his turning changed nothing important. Then there is no reason to forbid it, and שמואל would not need to tell us.

keyTerms.meaning: What is the case? What are the details?
If you say, if we suggest

phrases.english: What are the circumstances?

phrases.aramaic: אִילֵּימָא דְּאִי לָא הַפֵּךְ בֵּיהּ הֲוָה בְּשִׁיל —
phrases.english: If we say that if he had not turned it over, it would have cooked anyway,
it is obvious!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Asks for the exact case behind שמואל's ruling.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: In what case did שמואל say the turned meat is permitted?
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: First option: the meat would have cooked anyway. This is rejected as too obvious to need saying.

steps.title: If it would not have cooked without him, why is it permitted?
steps.stepSummary: The other option is that the meat would never have cooked without the גוי. But then it should be forbidden as בישולי גוים.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, isn't it a case where if he hadn't turned it, it would not have cooked? Then why is it permitted? It is cooking of גוים!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא tries the other option and finds that it makes שמואל's ruling hard to understand.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If the meat only got cooked because of the גוי, then he really did the cooking. That is exactly בישולי גוים, so it should be forbidden, not permitted. Both options seem to fail, so an in-between case is needed.

keyTerms.meaning: Food cooked by a non-Jew, which the רבנן forbade

phrases.aramaic: אֶלָּא לָאו דְּאִי לָא הַפֵּךְ לָא הֲוָה בְּשִׁיל,
phrases.english: Rather, is it not where if he had not turned it over, it would not have cooked?
Why is it permitted?
It is the cooking of gentiles!

steps.triggerLanguage: אֶלָּא לָאו דְּאִי לָא הַפֵּךְ לָא הֲוָה בְּשִׁיל
steps.relationToPreviousStep: After the first option is rejected as obvious, the second option seems to contradict the ruling.
steps.kashyaTarget: שמואל's ruling that the turned meat is permitted
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: If the meat only cooked because of the גוי, he is the real cook, so it should be forbidden as בישולי גוים.

steps.title: The גוי only made it cook faster
steps.stepSummary: The case is in between: the meat would have cooked in two hours, and the turning made it cook in one. Speeding up cooking does not make it בישולי גוים.
steps.simpleTranslation: It is needed for a case where, without the turning, it would have cooked in two hours, and now it cooks in one hour. You might have said that speeding up the cooking counts for something, so שמואל teaches us it does not.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers by finding a middle case where שמואל's ruling is neither obvious nor contradictory.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The meat would have cooked anyway, just more slowly. One might think that making it cook faster is a real part of cooking, so it should be forbidden. שמואל teaches that only speeding it up does not make it the גוי's cooking.

keyTerms.meaning: It is only needed for... (this specific case)

steps.whatToRemember: A גוי who only makes a ישראל's food cook faster does not make it בישולי גוים, according to שמואל.

phrases.english: No, it is necessary

phrases.aramaic: דְּאִי לָא הַפֵּךְ הֲוָה בְּשִׁיל בְּתַרְתֵּי שָׁעֵי,
phrases.english: where if he had not turned it over, it would have cooked in two hours,
and now it cooks in one hour.
Lest you say:
hastening the cooking is a significant matter,
he teaches us otherwise.
phrases.notes: The 'he' is שמואל, whose ruling this whole discussion is explaining.

steps.triggerLanguage: לָא צְרִיכָא, דְּאִי לָא הַפֵּךְ הֲוָה בְּשִׁיל בְּתַרְתֵּי שָׁעֵי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Resolves the two-sided problem by defining a middle case.
steps.terutzResolutionType: לא צריכא: narrows the ruling to a specific in-between case
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Speeding up the cooking is a real act of cooking, so the meat would be forbidden.
steps.terutzMaskana: Speeding up the cooking does not count; the meat stays permitted.

steps.title: Challenge from רבי יוחנן's rule about בן דרוסאי's food
steps.stepSummary: רבי יוחנן said food already cooked like בן דרוסאי's food is not בישולי גוים. That implies food not yet at that point is בישולי גוים, even if a ישראל started it.
steps.simpleTranslation: But didn't רבי אסי say in the name of רבי יוחנן: Anything that is cooked like the food of בן דרוסאי has no problem of בישולי גוים. This implies that if it is not yet like the food of בן דרוסאי, it does have a problem of בישולי גוים!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges the answer just given, using a teaching of רבי יוחנן.
steps.deeperAnalysis: By רבי יוחנן's rule, a ישראל's start only protects the food once it reached the barely-edible stage of בן דרוסאי. In שמואל's case, the meat might not have reached that stage when the גוי turned it, so it should be forbidden, even though he only sped it up.

keyTerms.meaning: But didn't he say...? (opens a challenge)
Food cooked just enough to be barely edible

steps.confusionAlert: רבי יוחנן's statement does not openly say 'forbidden'. The challenge comes from the implied opposite: if food at the בן דרוסאי stage is fine, food below that stage is not.

phrases.aramaic: וְהָאָמַר רַבִּי אַסִּי אָמַר רַבִּי יוֹחָנָן:
phrases.english: But didn't Rabbi Asi say that Rabbi Yoḥanan said:
Anything that is cooked like the food of ben Derosai,
phrases.notes: Food cooked only enough to be barely edible.

phrases.english: is not subject to the prohibition of the cooking of gentiles.
This implies that if it is not like the food of ben Derosai,
it is subject to the prohibition of the cooking of gentiles!

steps.triggerLanguage: וְהָאָמַר רַבִּי אַסִּי אָמַר רַבִּי יוֹחָנָן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Attacks the answer of step 22 that speeding up the cooking does not count.
steps.kashyaTarget: The explanation that a גוי who only speeds up cooking does not make it בישולי גוים
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: רבי יוחנן's rule implies that food below the בן דרוסאי stage becomes בישולי גוים when a גוי cooks it. Meat cooked faster by a גוי may not have reached that stage, so it should be forbidden.

steps.title: רבי יוחנן was talking about food that was not cooking at all
steps.stepSummary: רבי יוחנן's rule about food not yet cooked like בן דרוסאי's food is about a case where the ישראל left the meat in a basket and the גוי put it into the oven. In that case the גוי started the cooking.
steps.simpleTranslation: There, in רבי יוחנן's case, the ישראל put the meat in a basket, and a גוי took it and put it in the oven.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the question from step 23. It explains that רבי יוחנן was talking about a different kind of case.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In רבי יוחנן's case the meat was sitting in a basket, not cooking at all, and the גוי alone put it into the oven. There, being cooked like בן דרוסאי's food already is what decides it. In שמואל's case the ישראל already put the meat on the coals and the גוי only sped things up, so it stays permitted.

keyTerms.meaning: A basket, a place where food just sits and does not cook
Food already partly cooked, enough to be edible in a basic way

steps.confusionAlert: The two rulings do not argue. In שמואל's case the cooking already started with the ישראל. In רבי יוחנן's case the גוי started it.
steps.whyThisMatters: This gives a clear line for בישולי גוים: what matters is who started the cooking. If the גוי only helps food the ישראל already set to cook, it is permitted.

phrases.english: There,
phrases.notes: This means the case in רבי יוחנן's rule from the last step.

phrases.english: it is a case where he put it in a basket,
and a gentile took it
and put it in the oven.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the קשיא of step 23 by setting רבי יוחנן's rule in a different case.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Different case: the two statements deal with different facts
steps.terutzHavaAmina: רבי יוחנן's rule seemed to say any food not yet at בן דרוסאי's level is forbidden, even if a ישראל put it on the fire.
steps.terutzMaskana: רבי יוחנן means only a case where the food was not cooking at all and the גוי started the cooking. When the ישראל started it and the גוי only sped it up, it is permitted.

steps.title: A ברייתא supports שמואל: a גוי may turn over the meat
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא teaches that a ישראל may put meat on coals and a גוי may turn it over until the ישראל comes back from shul or the בית המדרש, with no concern. A second case starts: a woman puts a pot on the stove and a גויה comes over.
steps.simpleTranslation: It was also taught in a ברייתא: A ישראל may put meat on the coals, and a גוי may come and turn it over until the ישראל comes back from the בית הכנסת or the בית המדרש, and he does not need to worry. A woman may put a pot on the stove, and a גויה comes...
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a ברייתא that supports שמואל's ruling from step 19. The ברייתא then starts a second, similar case that continues on the next amud.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The first case in the ברייתא is almost the same as שמואל's case: the ישראל puts the meat on the fire and the גוי only turns it. The ברייתא says there is nothing to worry about, so the meat is not בישולי גוים. This matches the answer in step 22 that speeding up cooking the ישראל started is fine.

keyTerms.meaning: This is also taught (in a ברייתא), a phrase that brings support
He need not be concerned, it is permitted

steps.whatToRemember: If a ישראל starts the cooking and a גוי only helps it along, for example by turning the meat, the food is not בישולי גוים.

phrases.english: This is also taught in a baraita:

phrases.aramaic: מַנִּיחַ יִשְׂרָאֵל בָּשָׂר עַל גַּבֵּי גֶּחָלִים,
phrases.english: A Jew may put meat on the coals,
and a gentile comes and turns it over
until the Jew comes back
from the synagogue or from the study hall,
and he does not need to worry.

phrases.aramaic: שׁוֹפֶתֶת אִשָּׁה קְדֵירָה עַל גַּבֵּי כִּירָה,
phrases.english: A woman may put a pot on the stove,
and a gentile woman comes
phrases.notes: The sentence isn't finished here. The ברייתא keeps going on the next amud.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: After the challenge is answered, the גמרא brings a ברייתא that supports שמואל's original ruling.
steps.raayaObject: שמואל's ruling (step 19) that meat a ישראל put on coals and a גוי turned over is permitted.
steps.raayaSupportSource: A ברייתא: a ישראל puts meat on coals, a גוי turns it until the ישראל returns from shul or the בית המדרש, and there is no concern.
